title: How to work any LR question
summary: Read the argument first, find the conclusion, find the gap, predict, then eliminate with a reason. One routine for all 25 questions.

slides.title: Most arguments are broken on purpose
body: Almost every Logical Reasoning stimulus is an argument: some evidence, and a conclusion the author thinks it proves. On most questions the evidence does not quite prove it. There is a gap.
Your job is to read like a skeptic. Accept every premise as true, even if it sounds false in real life, and ask only one thing: does this evidence get all the way to that conclusion?
Flaw, assumption, weaken, strengthen and evaluate questions are all questions about that same gap. Find it once, before the answers, and five question types get easier at once.
slides.callout: Accept the premises. Attack the leap from premises to conclusion.

steps.label: Read the stimulus first
steps.do: Read the whole argument before the question stem, so you read it as an argument rather than hunting for one detail.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.do: Look for the claim everything else supports. Words like so, therefore, thus and clearly point to it; words like because, since and for point to evidence.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.do: Ask what the author took for granted to get from the evidence to the conclusion. Name it in a few words: a new term that appears only in the conclusion, a cause assumed from a correlation, a sample stretched to everyone.

steps.label: Read the stem, predict
steps.do: Now the stem tells you what to do with the gap: describe it (flaw), close it (assumption, strengthen), exploit it (weaken). Say what the right answer will roughly do before you read the choices.

steps.label: Eliminate with a reason
steps.do: Cross out each wrong choice for a reason you could say out loud: out of scope, wrong direction, too strong, describes the wrong part. Pick the survivor, not the one that sounds smartest.

slides.title: What each family does with the gap
head: Family
Question types
Your move
rows: Name the error in general terms.
Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen, Principle (justify)
Find the missing link or make it more likely.
Find a fact that widens the gap, or the question whose answer decides it.
Must Be True, Most Strongly Supported, Must Be False, Fill in the Blank
Stay inside the text and connect what it says.
Main Conclusion, Argument Part, Method, Parallel Reasoning
Point at Issue, Point of Agreement
Find the claim both speakers address, then compare their positions on it.
Find the fact that lets both be true.
slides.note: Inference questions are the exception: their stimulus is a set of facts, not an argument, so there is no gap to find.

slides.title: The routine on one question
slides.stimulus: Riverton's city council installed brighter streetlights on Elm Street last spring. Since then, reported bicycle thefts on Elm Street have fallen by 40 percent. Clearly, brighter lighting deters bicycle theft.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Several other streets in Riverton also had their older streetlights replaced with brighter ones last spring.
choices.B: Last spring, the bicycle racks on Elm Street were moved into a staffed parking garage.
choices.C: Most bicycle thefts in Riverton take place after dark.
choices.D: Bicycle ownership in Riverton rose slightly over the past year.
choices.E: Residents of Elm Street say they feel safer walking at night than they did before.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: “Clearly” marks it: brighter lighting deters bicycle theft. That is a causal claim.
steps.highlight: Clearly, brighter lighting deters bicycle theft.

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: After the new lights went in, thefts on Elm Street fell 40 percent. That is a before-and-after correlation.
steps.highlight: reported bicycle thefts on Elm Street have fallen by 40 percent

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: The author assumes nothing else changed on Elm Street at the same time. If something else did, the lights may have done nothing.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: For a weaken question, look for another change last spring that would cut thefts on its own.

why.A: Says nothing about what happened to thefts on those streets, so it neither helps nor hurts.
why.B: Correct. Bikes locked in a staffed garage are hard to steal. That is another cause for the drop, which the argument overlooked.
why.C: If thefts happen after dark, lighting is more likely to matter. This strengthens.
why.D: More bikes would make a drop in thefts more impressive, if anything. It does not weaken.
why.E: How safe residents feel is not evidence about what caused the drop in bicycle thefts.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Read the stimulus before the stem.
Accept every premise; attack only the leap.
Name the gap in a few words before you look at the choices.
The stem tells you what to do with the gap.
Eliminate for a reason you can say out loud.
Inference questions have no gap: stay inside the text.
